summary: Extends the SIP REFER method to use caller preferences from RFC 3840, so the sender of a REFER can describe the characteristics of the target that the induced request should reach. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4508 adds one thing to the SIP REFER method, which asks one phone to call another. The address of the third party in the Refer-To header can now carry extra labels, called feature tags, that say what that third party can do. The labels are the ones RFC 3840 defines, so the receiving phone already knows how to read them.

questions: how does refer-to carry feature tags
subtitle: How the sender of a SIP REFER can tell the recipient what the referred-to party can do.

tldr.problem: When one phone asks another to make a call to a third, the second phone had no way to know what the third could do, so it could not tell the user whether the transfer would work.
tldr.mechanism: The document lets the Refer-To header of a REFER request carry feature tags, the same labels RFC 3840 uses to describe a user agent's capabilities, such as isfocus, audio and video.
tldr.outcome: The receiving phone learns the target's capabilities before making the induced request. RFC 4508 was later updated by RFC 8217.

today: RFC 4508 was published in May 2006 as a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 8217. The extension is still how a REFER conveys the target's capabilities.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document extends the SIP REFER method defined in RFC 3515 to be used with feature parameters defined in RFC 3840.

Feature tags are used by a user agent to convey to another user agent information about capabilities and features. This information can be shared by a user agent using a number of mechanisms, including REGISTER requests and responses and OPTIONS responses. It can also be shared in the context of a dialog by inclusion with a remote target URI, that is, a Contact URI.

Feature tag information can be very useful to another user agent, and it is especially useful prior to the establishment of a session. For example, if a user agent knows, through an OPTIONS query, that the remote user agent supports both video and audio, the calling user agent might call offering video in the SDP. Another example is when a user agent knows that a remote user agent is acting as a focus and hosting a conference. In this case, the user agent might first subscribe to the conference URI and find out details about the conference prior to sending an INVITE to join.

This extension to the REFER method provides a mechanism by which the REFER-Issuer can provide this useful information about the REFER-Target's capabilities and functionality to the REFER-Recipient, by including feature tags in the Refer-To header field in a REFER request.
sections.plainLanguage: Before this change, the phone that receives the referral knows only an address. With it, the address can also say whether the far end handles video, hosts a conference, and so on.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content: The document introduces three terms to simplify discussions of the REFER method and its extensions. The REFER-Issuer is the user agent issuing the REFER request. The REFER-Recipient is the user agent receiving the REFER request. The REFER-Target is the user agent designated in the Refer-To URI.
sections.plainLanguage: Three roles: the one asking for the referral, the one that receives the request, and the one that ends up being called.

sections.title: The Refer-To Header Extension
sections.content:
The Refer-To grammar from RFC 3515 is extended. The original form is Refer-To = ("Refer-To" / "r") HCOLON ( name-addr / addr-spec ) *(SEMI generic-param), and it becomes Refer-To = ("Refer-To" / "r") HCOLON ( name-addr / addr-spec ) *(SEMI refer-param), where refer-param = generic-param / feature-param and feature-param is defined in section 9 of RFC 3840.

The document notes that if any URI parameters are present, the entire URI must be enclosed in angle brackets. If they are not present, all parameters after the URI are header parameters and not URI parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The header already accepted a list of parameters. This change says one of those parameters may be a feature tag, and warns that a URI parameter and a header parameter look the same unless the URI is put in angle brackets.

sections.title: The isfocus Feature Tag
sections.content:
The example shows how the isfocus feature tag can be used by the REFER-Issuer to tell the REFER-Recipient that the REFER-Target is a conference focus, and consequently that sending an INVITE will bring the REFER-Recipient into the conference.

The header is written as Refer-To: sip:conf44@example.com;isfocus.
sections.plainLanguage: One tag says the far end runs a conference. The receiving phone can then tell the user that picking up will join a conference rather than start a one-to-one call.

sections.title: Voice, Video and URI Parameters
sections.content:
The second example shows how a REFER-Issuer can tell the REFER-Recipient that the REFER-Target supports audio and video, and consequently that a video and audio session can be established by sending an INVITE to the REFER-Target. The header is written as Refer-To: "Alice's Videophone" <sip:alice@videophone.example.com> ;audio;video.

The third example shows how the REFER-Issuer can tell the REFER-Recipient that the REFER-Target is a voicemail server. The transport URI parameter is enclosed within the angle brackets so that it is not interpreted as a header parameter. The header is written as Refer-To: <sip:alice-vm@example.com;transport=tcp> ;actor="msg-taker";automata;audio.
sections.plainLanguage: Several tags can be given at once, and a tag that belongs to the address rather than to the header has to be kept inside the angle brackets so the two are not confused.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Feature tags can provide sensitive information about a user or a user agent. RFC 3840 cautions against providing sensitive information to another party. Once this information is given out, any use may be made of it, including relaying to a third party as in this specification.

A REFER-Issuer MUST NOT create or guess feature tags. A feature tag included in a REFER SHOULD be discovered in an authenticated and secure method, such as an OPTIONS response or from a remote target URI in a dialog, directly from the REFER-Target. It is RECOMMENDED that the REFER-Issuer includes in the Refer-To header field all feature tags that were listed in the most recent Contact header field of the REFER-Target.

A feature tag provided by a REFER-Issuer cannot be authenticated or certified directly from the REFER request, so the REFER-Recipient MUST treat the information as a hint. If the REFER-Recipient's application logic or the user's action depends on the presence of the expressed feature, the feature tag can be verified. For example, the REFER-Recipient can directly send an OPTIONS query to the REFER-Target over a secure connection, such as a mutually authenticated and integrity-protected one. This protects the REFER-Recipient against the sending of incorrect or malicious feature tags.
sections.plainLanguage: The tags are only a hint. Whoever sent them could have made them up, so the receiving phone must check them itself if it is going to act on them.

viz.caption: THE REFER-TO GRAMMAR, BEFORE AND AFTER

data.title: Refer-To header syntax
data.code:
Refer-To = ("Refer-To" / "r") HCOLON ( name-addr / addr-spec )
              *(SEMI generic-param)

becomes

Refer-To = ("Refer-To" / "r") HCOLON ( name-addr / addr-spec )
              *(SEMI refer-param)
refer-param = generic-param / feature-param
